Empirical Research Plan:  “How much of the post-1700 rise in population and urbanization can be traced to the Old-World arrival of the potato?”

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy:  Difference-in-Differences (multi-period) complemented by an event-study graph.

Why DID fits:  
• The potato represents a clearly timed, plausibly exogenous shock (first large-scale Old-World adoption ≈ 1700).  
• Geographic agro-climatic suitability for potatoes is predetermined by nature and differs sharply across countries.  
• Comparing high-suitability vs. low-suitability countries before and after 1700 isolates the causal “bite” of the new crop on demographic outcomes.

Formally:

Yct = αc + γt + β (SuitPotc × Postt) + Xct′δ + εct

where Yct ∈ {log population, log urban pop share}, SuitPotc is the share of land suitable for potato cultivation, Postt = 1 for t ≥ 1700, αc are country fixed effects, γt are century fixed effects, and Xct are time-varying controls.  β is the parameter of interest.

With seven centuries of data we will also estimate event-study coefficients:

Yct = αc + γt + Σk≠-1 βk (SuitPotc × 1{Century = k}) + Xct′δ + εct

(k = −3 for 1000,…,+2 for 1900; k = −1 (1600) is the omitted baseline).  Parallel pre-trends can then be visually and formally tested.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: SuitPotc = share of each country’s land that the FAO/GAEZ rates as agro-climatically suitable for potato cultivation (rain-fed, low-input).  
• (For robustness, we will discretise: “treated” = SuitPotc above the Old-World median.)

Control group  
• Countries whose SuitPotc is below the median (or zero).  
• All observations pre-1700 serve as additional implicit controls.

Treatment timing  
• Postt = 1 in 1700, 1800, 1900; 0 in 1000, 1400, 1500, 1600.

No RDD is involved; the running variable is geographic suitability, which is fixed—not a threshold.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel pre-trends.  Conditional on controls, high- and low-potato-suitability countries followed similar population/urbanisation trends before 1700.  
- Plausibility: We have four pre-periods (1000–1600) to test this directly.

A2. No time-varying omitted shock correlated with SuitPotc after 1700.  
- Plausibility: Major concurrent shocks (e.g., industrial revolution, colonial extraction, railways) were not determined by soil/climate suitability for potatoes.  We will control for other crop suitabilities, continent-century fixed effects, and pre-1700 slave exports to mitigate this concern.

A3. SuitPotc is exogenous to human choices and unaffected by the potato shock (immutability).  
- Plausibility: Climate zones and soil types are geologic.  Even if some land improvement occurred, the FAO classification is based on natural endowments, not realised usage.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country spillovers that violate SUTVA).  
- Plausibility: International migration flows were modest relative to country populations in 1700–1800; diffusion externalities bias toward zero if anything.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Main Threats and Mitigations  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Confounding New-World crops/inputs (maize, sweet potato, cassava).  
• Mitigation: Include interaction of Postt with each other New-World crop suitability share.  Estimate a triple-diff: (SuitPotato − SuitMaize − SuitSweetPotato)×Postt.

T2. Industrialisation or colonial extraction correlated with temperate-zone potato suitability (Europe).  
• Mitigation: (i) Add continent-century fixed effects; (ii) allow Europe-specific century trends; (iii) re-estimate dropping Western Europe altogether; (iv) control for Roman empire legacy, serfdom indicators, slave exports.

T3. Differential wars, plagues, or measurement error in early population counts.  
• Mitigation: (i) Cluster SEs at country level and drop known plague centuries (e.g., 1400) in robustness; (ii) run city-level analogue; (iii) placebo test using 1000–1500 “fake post” dummy.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Data loading ----
# Assume three CSVs in working directory
country   <- fread("country_century.csv")   # Pop, urban share, controls
suit      <- fread("country_suitability.csv") # Potato, maize, etc.
controls  <- fread("country_static_controls.csv")

# Merge
dat <- merge(country, suit, by = "iso3")
dat <- merge(dat, controls, by = "iso3")

# ---- 2. Variable construction ----
dat[, post1700  := as.integer(century >= 1700)]
dat[, log_pop   := log(population)]
dat[, log_urbs  := log(urban_share + 1e-6)]           # avoid log(0)
# Suitability shares are already in 0–1
dat[, potato_post := potato_suit * post1700]
dat[, maize_post  := maize_suit  * post1700]
dat[, swpot_post  := swpot_suit  * post1700]

# ---- 3. Main DID specification ----
spec_main <- feols(log_pop ~ potato_post + maize_post + swpot_post +
                   wheat_suit*post1700 + rice_suit*post1700 + # OW staples
                   avg_elev + rugged + dist_coast |
                   iso3 + factor(century),
                   data = dat, cluster = ~iso3)

summary(spec_main)

# ---- 4. Event-study ----
dat[, c_enumerated := factor(century)]     # keep as factor
event <- feols(log_pop ~ potato_suit:c_enumerated + # interactions with ALL periods
               maize_suit:c_enumerated   +
               swpot_suit:c_enumerated   +
               avg_elev + rugged + dist_coast |
               iso3 + factor(century),
               data = dat, cluster = ~iso3)

iplot(event, coef = "potato_suit:c_enumerated")  # pre-trend visual

# ---- 5. Robustness: drop Europe ----
dat_noeu <- dat[continent != "Europe"]
spec_noeu <- update(spec_main, data = dat_noeu)
summary(spec_noeu)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
Direction: β̂ < 0 for mortality, ⇒ β̂ > 0 for population size and urban share.  
Magnitude (back-of-envelope): Europe’s average potato suitability ≈ 0.30.  
If β ≈ 0.40, then moving from 0 to 0.30 suitability after 1700 raises log population by 0.12 (=12%), roughly one-third of the observed 35–40% Old-World population surge between 1700 and 1800.  Urban share elasticities should be slightly lower (≈ 0.25).

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually supported (0/1) ………………… 1  
C2: No differential anticipation of treatment ……………………. 1  
C3: No contemporaneous confounders correlated with SuitPot … 0  
C4: Exogenous, time-invariant treatment assignment ………… 1  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers across units) ………………………… 0  
Total (out of 5) …………………………………………………… 3  

Overall, while geography is plausibly exogenous and pre-trends testable, residual contemporaneous confounders and potential cross-border migration spillovers warrant caution; hence a score of 3/5.
